title: The Pi Verifier Agent
youtube_title: GPT-5.5 VERIFIED Opus 4.7: A Pi Coding Agent That REVIEWS Like YOU

codebase.note: The free public repo (disler/the-verifier-agent) is the basic version; the members-only 'souped-up' version adds specialized verifier experts and the gpt-image-2 skill. The local codebase (the-verifier-agent-system) is the fuller build: it ships four verifier personas (generic, sqlite, image, python), two read-only scripts, and the gpt-image-2 skill.

tactic.name: The Verifier Agent — spend tokens to save time; attack the review constraint with an agent that verifies agents
tactic.one_liner: Stop hand-checking every '✅ done.' Put a second, read-only agent behind your builder that decomposes its work into atomic claims, proves each one deterministically, and re-prompts the builder — unprompted — when a claim fails. You trade 2–5× the tokens for the one thing tokens can't buy back: your time.
tactic.why_uncomfortable: By the token-optimizer's math it looks pure waste — you double or 5× your spend on an agent that writes no code and often just says 'looks good.' Worse, you deliberately lock yourself OUT of your own verifier: its input bar is disabled, you cannot type at it, you cannot vibe-code a one-off fix. When it misses something, the only available move is to edit the persona, the script, or the prompt template — you are forced to template your engineering every single time. It removes the lowest-hanging fruit of the generative-AI age (fire a one-off prompt and move on) from the menu, and it pushes you out of the interactive back-and-forth loop most engineers are comfortable living in. Dan's framing: the discomfort is the mechanism.

mission: Cross the widening gap between the two camps of 2026 engineers. Camp A is stuck prompting back and forth with a single agent — in 2026 that will feel like hand-typing code did in 2025, and they will be far behind. Camp B builds multi-agent systems that scale: agents coordinating with agents, code stacked with agents to run longer threads of work. The verifier agent is the simplest, highest-leverage entry into Camp B — a brutally simple two-agent system that is the rare pattern which compounds on BOTH trust and scale at once. You are not building your application anymore; you are building the agentic system that builds and checks the application. '2026 is the year of trust': do you trust your agents to do what you ask — and at what scale?

phase_model.single_agent_prompting: Camp A — an engineer in the loop, prompting one agent back and forth, babysitting output, re-prompting by hand. The lowest-hanging fruit of the generative-AI age. Fast to start, but it does not scale and it does not compound.
phase_model.multi_agent_orchestration: Camp B — coordinated systems of specialized agents that operate better together than alone. NOT sub-agent delegation; orchestration. The verifier agent is the first, most important multi-agent system Dan says most engineers can build: one builder + one read-only verifier that watches, decomposes, proves, and corrects.
phase_model.the_delta: The delta from Camp A to Camp B is a second agent with a hard architectural separation between writing and checking, plus a harness you own so the separation is enforced (not merely prompted). One agent reviewing its own output is one perspective at one moment of compute; two coordinated agents give a second perspective, doubled compute, and specialization (the verifier has a domain script + read-only persona the builder lacks; the builder has write/edit/generate the verifier lacks).

core_concepts.name: The Verifier Agent (two-agent observer pattern)
core_concepts.plain_english: A normal interactive builder agent runs in your terminal; a sibling verifier agent runs in its own window with input disabled. After every builder turn, the verifier independently re-runs the work with read-only tools and, only if a check fails, prompts the builder back with a concrete correction. It closes the review-constraint feedback loop so you stop hand-checking every claim of success.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We have this very simple two-agent system where on completion of any prompt that executes, the verifier is kicking off and doing work."
core_concepts.misconception: That it's just sub-agent delegation or a fancier chat. It is not delegation — the builder doesn't even know the verifier exists. It's a top-down observer with a hard write/check separation, and the verifier only speaks up when a proof fails.

core_concepts.name: The two constraints: planning and reviewing
core_concepts.plain_english: If you're doing agentic engineering right, your time goes to exactly two things: how much you can plan, and how much you can review. Most engineers stall on review — half the day spent re-checking 'I created the table / added the FK / applied the migration.' The verifier collapses the review side into a parallel agent, and compounds the planning side too (every gap it can't verify becomes an explicit ask you template next time).
core_concepts.dan_words: "In agentic coding, there are two constraints... Planning and reviewing. If you're doing things right, you're spending your time planning and reviewing. With the verifier agent, we can improve our review constraint."
core_concepts.misconception: That 'reviewing' means reading the agent's prose summary. Review here is proving claims against actual state with deterministic tools — the agent's final message is a CLAIM, never proof.

core_concepts.name: Spend tokens to save time
core_concepts.plain_english: The verifier often burns 2–5× the builder's tokens per turn. If you optimize for tokens that's wasteful; if you optimize for TIME it's the highest-leverage trade there is. Tokens are cheap and getting cheaper; your time is not. You scale compute to scale impact.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Quite literally spending 5x tokens to make sure that I spend less of my time... How much is your time worth? If you ask me, your time is worth a ton."
core_concepts.misconception: That more tokens = more cost you should minimize. The equation is tokens-for-time: pay tokens to reclaim hours of review, and take that trade every time you can.

core_concepts.name: Atomic claims — the art of verification is decomposition
core_concepts.plain_english: Everything you prompt is a bundle of small axioms — units of information that can be proven true or false. 'I created the users table' is really five claims (table exists, columns/types, primary key, FK constraints, defaults). The verifier's persona forces it to pull each apart and prove each independently. A single PASS that hides three unchecked sub-claims is worse than three explicit FAILs.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Everything you prompt into your agents, they're all small axioms. They're small claims. They're units of information that can be proven true or proven false."
core_concepts.misconception: That checking 'did it work?' at the bundle level is verification. Granularity IS the value — the verdict is only trustworthy at the atomic level, each atom tied to a deterministic tool output.

core_concepts.name: Trust AND scale — the rare pattern that does both
core_concepts.plain_english: Most agentic moves trade one for the other: review more deeply and you slow down (scale down); push more compute and you erode trust in any single output. The verifier doesn't trade — it scales the work (more compute, more turns) AND increases trust (every atomic claim now has a deterministic check behind it before you ever read 'done'). More work + more proof, both axes at once.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The verifier sits at a very important middle ground between trust and scale. Most agents increase trust or scale, not both. The verifier does both."
core_concepts.misconception: That adding agents automatically raises the error rate. Only if you don't engineer them — with the right core four and a harness you control, the math flips: you open the same tool everyone opens, but your results are verified.

core_concepts.name: Template your engineering — by force
core_concepts.plain_english: The verifier is structurally un-promptable: its input bar is locked, so you cannot drop a one-off instruction into it. The only thing that drives it is the on-stop prompt template rendered against the builder's stop event. So when it misses something, you can't type a fix — you must improve the persona, the script, or the template. That solves the whole problem class, not the one instance you hit. The lock isn't friction for its own sake; it's the mechanism that makes templating a habit.
core_concepts.dan_words: "I cannot fall to the lowest-hanging fruit of the generative AI age. There's no vibe coding this stuff. I cannot just fire a one-off prompt... I am forced to template my engineering into my verifier agent."
core_concepts.misconception: That the input lock is a limitation to work around. It's the point — remove one-off prompting from the menu and the only action left is the one that compounds.

core_concepts.name: Built-in positive feedback loop (the flywheel)
core_concepts.plain_english: Every verifier Report ends with two engineered questions: 'What could you not verify?' and 'What do you need from me to verify this next time?' Whatever it couldn't prove becomes the exact next thing you encode into the script or persona. Verifier accuracy compounds with every prompt you write — a flywheel, not a one-off check.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is a positive feedback loop. It's a flywheel. I can then take the information given me here on what it could not verify... and I can template this into the agent's system prompt."
core_concepts.misconception: That a verifier that says 'I couldn't check X' has failed. That gap is the highest-value output — it names precisely what to template next.

core_concepts.name: Top-down observer — builder doesn't know the verifier exists
core_concepts.plain_english: The builder just runs. On every turn it emits lifecycle ticks (start / stop / error) over a private unix socket — never transcript content. The verifier pulls what it needs from the builder's session JSONL on disk and does its own verification. The only thing the verifier can push back is a corrective prompt via one tool.
core_concepts.dan_words: "On every prompt on the stop hook, the builder agent sends an event through a Unix socket... the verifier takes in the session file. Thanks to the Pi agent harness, we have full access to everything our builder agent has done."
core_concepts.misconception: That the two agents chat over the wire. They don't — the socket carries only lifecycle events + one corrective channel; the substance comes from reading the builder's session file slice for that turn.

core_concepts.name: Own your agent harness
core_concepts.plain_english: The verifier lives inside a custom Pi agent harness you fully control. That's what makes the input lock, the read-only persona, the bash policy, and the auto-spawn possible. Claude Code / Codex / Gemini / open-code all change underneath your feet on every update; a harness you own doesn't. Owning the harness is how you control the core four — context, model, prompt, tools.
core_concepts.dan_words: "There are many coding agents, there are many agent harnesses, but this one is yours. Fully customizable, adaptable, and it doesn't change underneath your feet as soon as a new update rolls out."
core_concepts.misconception: That this is a Pi advertisement. The transferable claim is: to build systems like this you need control over the harness's tool surface and lifecycle — whatever tool gives you that.

core_concepts.name: The bash tool is the most dangerous tool — lock it down
core_concepts.plain_english: Security vulnerabilities and agents-off-the-rails are both going parabolic. Bash is the single most dangerous tool you hand an agent. The verifier restricts bash to exactly one allowed script — the highest level of control — and layers read-only enforcement on top. If the model tries anything with bash other than the one script, it's fully blocked.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The bash tool is the most dangerous tool you can give your agents... this tool is a ticking time bomb. And so what I've done here in my verifier agent is I've restricted it to using just one script. This is the highest level of control you can give."
core_concepts.misconception: That prompting 'please be read-only' is enough. Enforcement is OUTSIDE the model — three independent layers (persona tools allowlist, tool-call bash override, read-only script/connection) all must be defeated before any state mutates.

core_concepts.name: Stack intelligence — it's AND, not OR
core_concepts.plain_english: Every model benchmark tests one model in isolation. From an engineer's view that's the missing piece: maximum intelligence isn't picking Opus 4.7 OR GPT-5.5 — it's Opus 4.7 AND GPT-5.5, coordinated and specialized. Real intelligence is combinations of models orchestrated together, which no benchmark measures but you can build.
core_concepts.dan_words: "It's not about GPT 5.5 or Opus 4.7. It's GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.7. It's an and, not an or... Stack intelligence. Orchestrate intelligence."
core_concepts.misconception: That you must chase the single 'best' model. The frontier is combinations — a builder model that writes and a different verifier model that checks each catch the other's misses.

core_concepts.name: One agent, one prompt, one purpose — and stack them
core_concepts.plain_english: A focused agent is a performant agent. Each verifier does exactly one job (image readability, or SQLite integrity, or Python types/tests) and does it well. Because the verifier is independent of the builder, you can stack more than one specialized verifier behind the same builder — an extension layer of specialized validation on top of whatever your primary agent is.
core_concepts.dan_words: "One agent, one prompt, one purpose. A focused agent is a performant agent... I can just continue to stack up these verifier agents to focus on one specific thing."
core_concepts.misconception: That one giant do-everything verifier is better. Specialization beats breadth here; the SQLite verifier stays silent on image work and vice versa (each domain persona has a relevance gate).

core_four.context: What the verifier can see: the builder's session JSONL on disk (read only the [start..end] slice for the turn, passed as line offsets so it never scans a multi-MB file), the original user prompt (forwarded on the start/stop event so the verifier grounds its checks in what you actually ASKED for, not just what the builder claimed), and the repo files via read/grep/find/ls.
core_four.model: A DIFFERENT model from the builder, on purpose — stacked intelligence. In the video the builder is Opus 4.7; the image verifier ran GPT-5.5 and the SQLite verifier ran GLM 5.1. The persona's `model:` field pins the verifier model regardless of the user's global default. (On disk today all four personas declare `openai/gpt-5.5`; the video's verify_sqlite.md showed `z-ai/glm-5.1` — the model is a one-line swap, which is the whole point.)
core_four.prompt: Two templated layers: the persona system prompt (rendered once at spawn with BUILDER_SESSION_ID / SOCKET_PATH / etc.) and the per-cycle verify_on_stop.md user prompt (rendered on every stop event with TURN_INDEX, the line-offset slice, and the original user prompt). You improve behavior by editing these templates — never by typing at the verifier.
core_four.tools: Deliberately narrowed: read, grep, find, ls, bash, plus the extension-provided verifier_prompt (the ONLY outbound channel to the builder). No write, no edit — the model can't call what isn't registered. For domain personas, bash is further locked to a single allowed script.
core_four.why_it_matters: When something goes wrong, you can't fire a one-off prompt — you're forced to improve one or more of the core four. Dan: 'I'm effectively forced to improve one or more of the core four, context, model, prompt, or tools.' Owning the harness is what lets you engineer all four axes precisely enough that adding a second agent lowers your error rate instead of raising it.

example_a_image.recipe: just vimg  (≡ pi -e verifiable.ts -e cross-agent.ts --verifiable --verifier-agent verify_image)
flow: Prompt the builder: 'run prime, then run skill gpt-image-2, generate arch.jpg to concisely describe the architecture of the verifier two-agent system.' /prime loads essential codebase context.

Builder (Opus 4.7) reads the gpt-image-2 SKILL, then writes a highly detailed image prompt and runs generate_gpt_image.py (~75s). One agent prompting another model — Opus templating a prompt for GPT Image 2.
On the builder's stop event, the verifier (GPT-5.5) kicks off UNPROMPTED. Hands off the keyboard.

The verifier reads arch.jpg, decomposes the request into atomic visual claims (exists, depicts the two-agent system, correct format/location, and ≤ MAX_TEXT_ELEMENTS=10 distinct text blocks), and checks each.

It finds the diagram violates the readability contract — too many distinct text blocks (bullet-list-heavy 'top-down observer' draft). It calls verifier_prompt with a concrete fix ('regenerate with fewer than 10 contiguous text blocks; combine labels; use icons instead of internal bullet lists').
The builder receives the correction as a follow-up user message and regenerates a simplified icon-based diagram (exactly 7 text blocks).

Next cycle: STATUS VERIFIED, CONFIDENCE PERFECT, 7/7 atomic claims, green bar. The human never touched the keyboard for the correction. The ≤ 10-block rule lives in the persona and is enforced on every image forever.
Dan then pushes a second round ('add us — the ones prompting the builder — into the picture') to show the loop runs again on an edit.
just shows the recipe list; just vsql boots the builder + auto-spawns the SQLite verifier in a sibling window.
Prompt the builder: 'find all SQLite DBs in this repo, breakdown tables, columns, and relationships.' Opus 4.7 finds tmp/mock_shop.db and tmp/mock_shop_backup.db and reports tables/columns/FKs.

The verifier (GLM 5.1) decomposes the work into 16 atomic claims and proves each via the ONE allowed script: PRAGMA index_list(...), SELECT count(*) per table, PRAGMA integrity_check → 'ok', FK reference checks.
Result: 16/16 verified, STATUS VERIFIED, CONFIDENCE PERFECT, green bar. No feedback needed — the verifier stays silent when nothing fails.

The verifier is restricted: bash is locked to `uv run --script .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py` only — anything else is blocked at the tool-call layer, and the script opens the DB `mode=ro&immutable=1`.

Token point: the Opus builder spent ~1% of context; the GLM verifier spent ~2× the builder's tokens (spend tokens to save time). Dan: this SQLite agent could be your Postgres / MySQL / MongoDB agent — swap the script + persona.

the_report_contract.status_line: STATUS: verified | failed | unsure — parsed by the verifier extension out of the '## Report' block of the verifier's last assistant message.

confidence_ladder.meaning: Every atomic claim verified with deterministic output; zero gaps; no verifier_prompt called.
All checked passed; 1–2 minor non-blocking unverifiable gaps.
No failures, but significant unverifiable gaps.
≥1 claim failed AND verifier_prompt was called — the system working as designed.
Could not verify at all (no oracle/fixture/ambiguous) — escalating to human.

report_sections: What did you verify? (each atomic claim + exact tool output + PASS/FAIL)
What could you not verify? (why — missing oracle/harness/fixture/ambiguous)
What feedback did you give? (paraphrase of the verifier_prompt message, or 'none')
What do you need from me to verify this next time? (the flywheel input)
Verification metadata (turn_index, atomic_claims_total / verified / failed / unverified, duration)
the_report_contract.escalation: Loop repeats up to max_loops (default 3, per persona). On the 4th attempt the builder surfaces a 'verifier failed N times — escalating to human' message instead of auto-injecting another correction.

three_read_only_layers.layer_1_persona_tools: The persona's `tools:` field is exactly `read, grep, find, ls, bash, verifier_prompt`. The launcher passes it to `pi --tools`, so Pi's runtime never registers write/edit for the verifier process. The model can't call what isn't there.
three_read_only_layers.layer_2_bash_policy: For domain personas that declare `bash_policy: {mode: script-only, allowed_script, runner}`, a pi.on('tool_call') hook blocks any bash command that doesn't start with `<runner> <allowed_script>`. The block reason is a structured teaching message ('the error message is the documentation') so the agent self-corrects.
three_read_only_layers.layer_3_script_readonly: verify_sqlite.py opens the DB with `mode=ro&immutable=1` and enforces a PRAGMA allowlist (only introspective PRAGMAs); dot-commands route through `sqlite3 -readonly`. verify_python.py only runs check-only tools (uvx ty / ruff check / ruff format --check / pytest). Every refusal is structured JSON `{error, received, reason, allowed, hint}` with a non-zero exit.
three_read_only_layers.socket_auth: The /tmp/pi-verifier/ directory is chmod 0700 — only the owning UID can connect. That is the authentication (no token to leak in ps).
three_read_only_layers.not_a_sandbox: Threat model caveat: the verifier still runs as your user. This locks down the VERIFIER as a source of mutation; a malicious builder-side prompt that gets the BUILDER to run rm -rf is a separate (builder) permission concern. Don't load untrusted personas — layers 1 and 2 are configured by the persona file.

step_by_step_demo: (0:00–1:35) Framing: April 2026's record model-release velocity (Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, DeepSeek V4, GLM 5.1, Kimi K2.6, Qwen). Model performance is no longer the bottleneck — you are. Two Pi agents sit side by side (builder Opus 4.7 right, verifier GPT-5.5 left) and 'this harness takes no input' — something's weird.
(1:35–2:07) Image example begins. Prompt the builder: run /prime, then run skill gpt-image-2, generate arch.jpg to describe the verifier two-agent architecture.
(2:07–3:05) Builder (Opus 4.7) primes, reads the gpt-image-2 skill, and fires generate_gpt_image.py with a highly detailed prompt. ~75s. One agent prompting another model.
(3:05–3:35) On the builder's stop, the verifier (GPT-5.5) kicks off UNPROMPTED. Hands off the keyboard. It reads the generated image and starts validating claims.

(3:35–4:10) The verifier finds a problem and calls verifier_prompt — 'my verifier agent just prompted my builder agent.' Feedback mode: the correction fires a new builder turn, completely unprompted by the human.

(4:10–5:10) In VS Code, look at the first (text-dense 'top-down observer') arch.jpg before it's overwritten — Dan clones it as arch copy.jpg. The Report: STATUS failed, CONFIDENCE feedback — the image is legible but violates the readability contract (> 10 distinct text blocks; MAX_TEXT_ELEMENTS=10).

(5:10–6:10) Break down the failed Report: every atomic claim listed, the readability rule that fired, and the corrective feedback the verifier sent (regenerate with fewer than 10 blocks; combine labels; use icons).
(6:10–7:10) The builder regenerated a simplified diagram. Now a clean green bar: VERIFY_IMAGE VERIFIED / PERFECT, 7/7 atomic claims. The verifier did NOT need to re-prompt.

(7:10–9:00) Value props written out: spend tokens to save time; the review constraint; the positive feedback loop ('what could you not verify / what do you need from me'); template your engineering by force (un-promptable harness). Second round: 'add us into the picture' runs the loop again on an edit.

(9:40–12:15) The two constraints of agentic coding — planning and reviewing. The verifier attacks review by teaching an agent exactly how you verify. One agent, one prompt, one purpose. You can stack specialized verifiers.

(12:15–14:05) The customized system prompt: a persona with rules (search 'max text elements') and a fixed Report format including 'what could you not verify' and 'what do you need from me.' This is what owning the harness lets you do.

(14:05–16:35) Template your engineering as a habit — by force. The input is locked; you can't vibe-code the verifier; the only fix is improving one of the core four. The widening gap between Camp A (stuck prompting) and Camp B (building systems).
(16:55–17:35) SQLite example. `just` shows recipes; `just vsql` boots builder + SQLite verifier (GLM 5.1). Prompt: find all SQLite DBs, break down tables, columns, relationships.

(17:35–19:35) The verifier is independent of the builder — an extension layer of specialized validation. It decomposes the work into atomic claims (find all DBs; break down tables; columns; relationships) and proves each.
(19:35–21:05) Restricted bash: this verifier can run only one script. Bash is the most dangerous tool — lock it down. SQLite agent → could be your Postgres/MySQL/MongoDB agent.

(21:05–22:40) 16/16 atomic claims verified, PERFECT. Token point: Opus ~1%, GLM ~2× the builder — spending 2× compute to increase trust by validating atomic claims. This system compounds with every prompt.
(23:00–25:38) What's missing from every benchmark: they test one model in isolation. Real intelligence is combinations — GPT-5.5 AND Opus 4.7, not OR. Stack intelligence; own your agent harness.

(25:38–30:25) TAC / Agentic Horizon pitch: vibe coding is the floor, agentic engineering is the ceiling; operate on the agentic layer, not the application. Two versions of the verifier shipped (free GitHub basic; members souped-up with experts + gpt-image-2 skill).

(30:25–32:51) Channel focus: trust and scale. 2026 is the year of trust. The verifier sits at the middle ground and does both. Next up: agentic security — damage from within, the bash tool as the biggest hole in everyone's agent.

prerequisites_tools: Python 3.11+ (verifier scripts use inline PEP 723 headers)
tmux (the verifier runs in a sibling tmux window)
sqlite3 CLI on PATH (for the SQLite verifier's dot-commands)
Pi Coding Agent (`pi`) authenticated against an LLM provider
just (every workflow recipe runs through the justfile)
An LLM provider API key in a project-local .env (OPENAI_API_KEY is canonical for the default gpt-5.5 verifier; OPENAI_API_KEY also powers the gpt-image-2 skill)
macOS or Linux (Windows-native untested — use WSL)
what_student_must_internalize: The verifier attacks the REVIEW constraint — one of the only two constraints (planning + reviewing) that bind agentic engineering. That's why it's high-leverage.
Verification = decomposition. Break the builder's claims into atomic propositions and prove each against actual state with a deterministic tool. The agent's prose is a claim, never proof.
You spend tokens to save time. 2–5× the tokens per turn is the correct trade when your time is the scarce resource.
The verifier is the rare pattern that compounds trust AND scale simultaneously — most agentic moves trade one for the other.
The un-promptable harness forces you to template your engineering: fixes go into the persona / script / prompt, never a one-off. That solves the whole class, not the instance.
Read-only is enforced by architecture (three independent layers), not by asking the model nicely. Bash is the most dangerous tool — lock it to one script.
It's AND, not OR: a builder model + a different verifier model beats either alone. Stack and orchestrate intelligence; benchmarks that test one model miss this.
The builder never knows the verifier exists (top-down observer): lifecycle ticks over a socket, substance pulled from the session JSONL slice.
Own your harness — that control is what makes the input lock, tool narrowing, bash policy, and auto-spawn possible; other tools change under your feet.
The Report's 'what could you not verify / what do you need from me' is a flywheel: every gap is the next thing you template. Verifier accuracy compounds.
common_weak_student_failures: Reading the verifier as sub-agent delegation. It's an observer with a hard write/check separation — the builder doesn't know it exists, and it only speaks when a proof fails.
Optimizing for tokens and concluding the verifier is 'wasteful.' The trade is tokens-for-time; the whole point is spending 2–5× tokens to reclaim hours of review.
Trying to 'just tell the verifier' to fix a miss. Its input is locked by design — the only fix is editing the persona/script/template. Fighting the lock misses the lesson.
Accepting a single top-level PASS as verification. Without atomic decomposition a PASS can hide three unchecked sub-claims; granularity is the value.
Assuming 'read-only persona' means the prompt says be careful. Enforcement is outside the model — three layers — and 'please be read-only' alone is not security.
Chasing the single best model. The frontier is combinations — builder model AND a different verifier model — which no single-model benchmark can show.
Treating 'what could you not verify' as failure noise instead of the flywheel input that tells you exactly what to template next.

Confusing the video's models with the shipped defaults: the video ran GLM 5.1 / GPT-5.5 verifiers; the on-disk personas declare openai/gpt-5.5. The model is a one-line swap — don't hard-code your mental model to either.
Expecting the free GitHub repo to include every domain verifier. v1's README says only SQLite ships; the members/local build adds image + python + generic. Check what your clone actually contains.
teach_back_prompt: Explain to a colleague, without notes: (1) which of the two constraints of agentic coding the verifier attacks, and why decomposing the builder's work into atomic claims — each tied to a deterministic tool output — is what makes 'review' trustworthy; (2) why the verifier is the rare pattern that raises BOTH trust and scale, when most agentic moves trade one for the other; (3) how the un-promptable, input-locked harness forces you to template your engineering, and why 'the error message is the documentation' matters for the bash policy. Finish by resolving the apparent paradox: how does spending 2–5× the tokens on an agent that writes no code make you FASTER — and why is it AND (builder + verifier model), not OR?

retrieval_questions.q: What are the two constraints of agentic coding, and which one does the verifier attack?
retrieval_questions.a: Planning and reviewing. The verifier attacks the review constraint by teaching an agent exactly how you verify and re-checking every turn deterministically.

retrieval_questions.q: What is an 'atomic claim' and why decompose?
retrieval_questions.a: The smallest proposition with an unambiguous truth value (e.g. 'the users table has a PRIMARY KEY on id'). Decomposition is the art of verification — a single PASS that hides three unchecked sub-claims is worse than three explicit FAILs; each atom must cite a deterministic tool output.

retrieval_questions.q: State the core trade the verifier makes.
retrieval_questions.a: Spend tokens to save time. The verifier burns ~2–5× the builder's tokens per turn; if you optimize for time (your scarce resource) rather than tokens (cheap), it's the highest-leverage trade there is.

retrieval_questions.q: Why is the verifier called the rare 'trust AND scale' pattern?
retrieval_questions.a: Most agentic moves trade one for the other (review deeper → slower; more compute → less trust in any single output). The verifier scales the work AND increases trust — every atomic claim now has a deterministic check before you read 'done.'

retrieval_questions.q: Why is the verifier's input bar locked, and what does that force?
retrieval_questions.a: So you cannot fire a one-off prompt at it. The only way to fix a miss is to edit the persona, script, or prompt template — which solves the whole problem class, not the instance. It makes templated engineering a habit by force.

retrieval_questions.q: Name the three independent read-only layers.
retrieval_questions.a: (1) Persona tools allowlist — no write/edit registered; (2) tool-call bash policy — bash must start with `<runner> <allowed_script>` or it's blocked with a teaching message; (3) the script itself — SQLite opened mode=ro&immutable=1 + PRAGMA allowlist, Python tools run check-only.

retrieval_questions.q: How does the builder communicate with the verifier, and what crosses the wire?
retrieval_questions.a: The builder emits lifecycle ticks (start/stop/error) over a private unix socket at /tmp/pi-verifier/<sid>.sock — NO transcript content. The verifier pulls the turn's slice from the builder's session JSONL on disk; the only thing it can push back is a corrective prompt via the verifier_prompt tool.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the readability rule in the image example, and what happened when it fired?
retrieval_questions.a: MAX_TEXT_ELEMENTS = 10 distinct text blocks per image. The first (bullet-heavy) diagram exceeded it, so the verifier failed the readability claim, called verifier_prompt with a concrete fix, the builder regenerated a 7-block icon diagram, and the next cycle came back VERIFIED / PERFECT — no human keystroke.

retrieval_questions.q: Why 'AND, not OR' when picking models?
retrieval_questions.a: Every benchmark tests one model in isolation; maximum intelligence comes from combinations — a builder model plus a DIFFERENT verifier model (e.g. Opus 4.7 builds, GPT-5.5 or GLM 5.1 verifies), each catching the other's misses. Stack and orchestrate intelligence.

retrieval_questions.q: What two questions end every Report, and why do they matter?
retrieval_questions.a: 'What could you not verify?' and 'What do you need from me to verify this next time?' They are the flywheel — each gap names exactly what to template into the script/persona next, so verifier accuracy compounds with every prompt.

retrieval_questions.q: Which tool does Dan call the 'most dangerous,' and how is it controlled?
retrieval_questions.a: The bash tool ('a ticking time bomb'). The verifier restricts it to exactly one allowed script via a tool-call hook — the highest level of control — and blocks anything else, feeding the block reason back as a teaching message.

retrieval_questions.q: What does 'own your agent harness' unlock that a stock coding tool doesn't?
retrieval_questions.a: The input lock, the tool-surface narrowing (no write/edit), the bash policy, custom personas, and auto-spawn — all require harness control. Stock tools (Claude Code / Codex / Gemini / open-code) change under your feet; a harness you own doesn't.

Claude Code offers hooks (PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop), a permission allowlist, and the Agent SDK for programmatic multi-agent control — the current idiom for building the same shape outside Pi.

A modern reader should know the verifier is the starter multi-agent system; the ceiling (teams, orchestration, the codebase singularity) is far higher and is developed across AH/MA.
